Chapter 9: Writing the Story—Truth, Memory, and the Act of Bearing Witness.
You know, there comes a time when making sense of the past just can't wait any longer. For the law student, that moment showed up late at night, surrounded by stacks of old notebooks and worn case files. The urge to write felt almost impossible to ignore—not just to jot down what happened, but to actually understand it.
The first words didn’t come easy. They kind of stumbled onto the page. Memories drifted in, some crystal clear, others faded by time. The law student wrote about the trial, about the family, and about how that case changed the way they saw everything.
Writing became more than just a record. It turned into a way to bear witness—to honor both the pain and the resilience of everyone involved.
At some point, a friend—someone who always knew how to listen—read an early draft. She offered gentle feedback, pointing out spots where the story felt a little too distant, almost clinical. “Let yourself feel it,” she said. “That’s where the truth is.” It was a wake-up call. Telling the story honestly meant showing some vulnerability, letting that pain show through.
Most of us, honestly, we’re scared to revisit the hardest parts of our lives. There’s always that fear that the memories might just be too much, that the pain will come rushing back. But the law student discovered that writing—even the painful parts—was actually a way to take the story back. It was a way to say, “This happened. It mattered. I survived.”
It wasn’t always smooth. Some days, the words just wouldn’t come. Sometimes the memories were just too raw. But then, there were those rare moments of clarity—when the pieces started to fit together in ways they never had before.
And through it all, the law student came to realize something important: bearing witness—telling the truth, even when it’s messy—is its own kind of justice.
